# Frame forwarding SDK

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

The `@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit/frame-forwarding` package connects an authorized native producer to Electron Main without routing pixels through DSH Host. This public Kit subpath contains Node/TypeScript producer and receiver APIs backed by the same Electron-independent C/C++ SDK. Its payload includes explicitly listed C/C++ build sources; source globs and source maps are excluded. macOS uses IOSurface with Mach port transfer; Windows uses D3D11 shared NT handles and an owner-only named pipe. Separate browser and Electron subpaths provide presentation and texture ownership; consumers own authorization and application commands.

Installing Kit with `--omit=optional` provides the SDK without Office engines or the Windows Office pipe dependency Koffi. Normal installation retains both optional dependency selections. Neither SDK installation nor SDK communication compiles or downloads binaries.

## Receiver

Create one `createBudget(maxBytes)` per window and pass it to every `createReceiver({ maxFrames, maxBytes, budget, displayAdapter, readbackTimeoutMs, framePolicy }, onEvent)`. Each receiver is one channel, and its `tx` is an opaque, serializable credential. Pass `tx` to the producer process, for example from the parent that starts it; any process holding a copy may connect, and copying it revokes nothing. The credential must never reach the Renderer, logs or diagnostics.

Frame events carry `transport: "shared-texture"`, an eight-byte native handle, the producer's `frameId`, and a receiver-owned `deliveryId`. Call `release(deliveryId)` only after Electron reports `allReferencesReleased`; queue submission and frame timeout do not release consumer ownership. Delivery IDs remain distinct when a producer reuses a released frame ID. Duplicate releases return false. `close()` asynchronously drains submitted GPU work and joins the owned workers; delivered resources remain retained until release or receiver destruction. A stalled GPU can keep close pending; cancellation never frees resources still used by that GPU.

Windows shared-texture receivers require the compositor’s actual adapter LUID in `displayAdapter`; creating one without it fails. The producer reports its device LUID during authentication, and the receiver verifies it against each texture. For matching adapters, keyed producer textures are imported directly; legacy textures are copied into a receiver-owned shared target. `sourceKeyedMutex` reports the actual source descriptor, independent of the handshake declaration. For different adapters, a native worker reads back the entire source texture and uploads its premultiplied BGRA pixels into a shared texture on the compositor’s adapter. JavaScript receives only its handle. `adapterId` identifies the source; `presentationAdapterId` identifies the exported texture’s adapter and is null for macOS IOSurface.

The receiver’s Windows target uses a keyed mutex recognized by Chromium to order GPU access; Electron’s reference-release callback controls lifetime but does not replace this synchronization. Cross-adapter copies preserve row pitch and return source credit as soon as the readback GPU copy completes; the independent target remains held until Electron releases its delivery. Same-adapter copying and macOS IOSurface retain source credit through delivery release. GPU completion uses reusable fence events when supported and bounded query polling otherwise. `readbackTimeoutMs` bounds native frame preparation and delivery; timeout or cancellation stops new work while retaining submitted copies until GPU completion or device removal. Worker termination and receiver garbage collection use the same asynchronous cleanup.

[Chromium 152 acquires key 0 with `INFINITE`](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/24072c1aa400ec4a89dc738b6b6acd12a8589b6f/gpu/command_buffer/service/dxgi_shared_handle_manager.cc#L129). Before direct handoff, the receiver worker performs a bounded acquire/release readiness check. This moves a possible CPU wait to that worker without copying pixels; it does not impose a timeout on Chromium. A producer must release before submitting and must not access the surface until credit returns. A producer that violates this after the check can still stall Chromium or trigger its GPU watchdog.

Shared-texture `framePolicy` defaults to `ordered`, preserving independent request/reply frames such as Office tiles. Continuous streams may select `latest`: a completed relay readback replaces the frame whose upload has not begun, with at most one pending frame and one upload in progress. Two staging slots allow source copying while a prepared frame waits for a target. Held targets stop further uploads; ordered delivery also stops readback when both staging slots are occupied. Under `ordered`, a frame the producer marked replaceable replaces the replaceable frames whose upload has not begun and leaves other frames queued, so one receiver serves request/reply frames and a stream.

The byte budget reserves one surface per macOS allocation or declared Windows same-adapter keyed allocation. A legacy same-adapter allocation reserves a source plus target. The optional hello capability permits the smaller reservation; a declared keyed producer that supplies a non-keyed texture is rejected. An undeclared keyed source can still be imported directly, with the conservative legacy reservation. Relay reserves up to `N = maxFrames` source textures, `N` independent targets, and two staging textures. Target and staging capacity tracks the connection's largest requested frame; source and pool growth receive one atomic budget grant. Relay limits each frame to `maxBytes / (2N + 2)` bytes and advertises `N` times that allowance to the producer. With three frames and 256 MiB, three 4K BGRA sources plus the five receiver textures reserve 253.125 MiB. Idle storage retains its reservation; closing frees independent pool slots while each held target retains its own budget until release. Renderer queues and canvas storage have separate limits; this budget is not a process-memory ceiling.

A channel serves one producer connection at a time. Each `connected` event carries an increasing `connectionId` that the channel never reuses; every connection event names it. `send(connectionId, json)` queues a bounded control message for that connection without blocking Main on native I/O, and throws once that connection is no longer connected. Producer messages arrive as `message` events. While a producer is connected, other candidates are refused with `channel-busy`; a connected producer is never preempted, even when it stops responding. After it closes, fails or its process exits, the channel emits `disconnected` and drains: the connection keeps its frames, allocations, budget and GPU relay state until every delivered frame is released and its GPU work completes, then emits `drained`. During the drain one authenticated successor waits for its ready and further candidates are refused with `channel-busy`; the successor's own deadline and cancellation still apply, and a successor that gives up frees its place. Frame and allocation IDs belong to their connection, so late releases of an old connection do not affect a successor reusing the same IDs, and credit returns only to the connection that sent the frame. `drain-blocked` reports GPU work whose completion is unknown: its resources and budget stay retained and the drain waits without a timeout. `rejected` reports a refused candidate, and `failed` means the channel stopped accepting producers. `close()` withdraws the credential, refuses a waiting successor and ends the current connection. Frames discarded before delivery release their native resources; delivered frames still require explicit release after closure. The OS-reported peer process is checked per physical connection for packet origin and handle duplication only; it grants no access.

Producers and receivers of protocol version 1 declare transferable channels in their handshake. A receiver refuses a producer without that declaration with `transferable-tx-required`, and a producer refuses a receiver whose ready carries no connection ID, so builds that bind producers by PID cannot interoperate with these sources. A producer of another protocol version is refused with `protocol-mismatch`, naming both versions.

Producers also declare that every handle they name belongs to them. On Windows a frame carries a handle value in the producer's process, and the receiver duplicates it from that process with the access it opened when the producer connected; a value that names no handle of a live producer ends the connection without touching any receiver handle, and a producer that exited took its handles with it, so its connection ends as lost. A receiver refuses a producer without the declaration with `producer-local-handles-required`, and ready echoes the declarations the receiver accepted, so a producer refuses a receiver that would read its handle values as handles of its own. Builds of 0.2.2 and earlier therefore cannot interoperate with these sources in either direction. A receiver that sandboxes its producers can keep this scheme, since only the receiver needs access to the other process.

On Windows, CPU relay retains one imported texture per allocation across staging slots. Reuse requires the NT handle to name the same object and dimensions to match; every frame still acquires key 0 before copying. Allocation retirement drops cached imports before returning credit, while pending copies retain their active source until completion. Systems without `CompareObjectHandles` continue opening and validating each frame.

## Node/TypeScript producer

Import `createProducer` from `@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit/frame-forwarding` inside the owning Node process. Pass the channel's `tx`, `maxPendingOperations`, and `operationTimeoutMs`. `ready` resolves once the channel's ready arrives, which waits while a previous producer drains, and rejects with a message starting `channel-busy` while another producer is connected; `operationTimeoutMs` bounds that wait. Register explicit `close()` with the owning plugin's disposal: it stops new operations, discards unsubmitted surfaces and disconnects, and its completion means the local sender is closed. A successor's `ready` marks the completed handoff. The [TypeScript API](index.d.ts) defines operations and resource ownership.

A dedicated native worker serializes connection, uploads, mutex waits and submission. A separate polling thread wakes it on credit and control events; acquisition does not poll on a timer. Accepted operations may queue before readiness; excess ordinary operations reject, including control messages. Discard has one reserved queue slot per owned lease so a full queue cannot prevent release. Pending acquisitions wait for credits without blocking worker execution. Acquisition timeout rejects that request without closing the producer. Transport or uncertain GPU completion failures close the connection. `closed` resolves after queued operations settle and the worker and client are destroyed. Event-listener exceptions are contained; listeners remain responsible for their own diagnostics. Worker termination uses asynchronous native cleanup. Set `DSH_FRAME_FORWARDING_DIAGNOSTICS=1` to report contained producer callback exceptions to stderr.

`acquire(width, height)` returns an explicit surface lease. Await `writeBgra(buffer, stride)`, then `submit(frameId, metadata)` or `discard()`; surface `close()` is a discard alias. Busy or consumed surfaces reject reuse. Garbage collection never grants frame credit. Submission consumes the lease, but the underlying texture remains unavailable until the receiver releases its frame.

CPU uploads borrow a non-shared Node Buffer until the returned promise settles. During that time callers must not modify it, detach it or transfer its backing ArrayBuffer. Row stride may exceed the packed row width. The binding retains the Buffer and avoids an intermediate binding copy; the C SDK still copies or uploads those bytes. CPU upload is not GPU zero-copy.

## C/C++ producer

Include `include/dsh_frame_forwarding.h` and link the matching `libdsh_frame_forwarding_sdk.a` or `dsh_frame_forwarding_sdk.lib`, or build the sources listed in `sdk.json`. The API has no Node or Electron dependency. Poll on one thread; acquisition, writing, submission and discard may run on another. Callers must serialize use of the same graphics context. Interrupt polling, join that thread, and close the client after all its API calls return.

The only public C header is `include/dsh_frame_forwarding.h`. The Graphite WebGPU adapter in `src/graphite-interop-internal.hxx` and `src/graphite-interop.cc` (`dsh::graphite::detail`) is an internal engine implementation and is not an SDK API. It waits for submitted GPU work to complete before publishing a frame; failed completion retains the allocation until the client closes.

On Windows, `dsh_frame_forwarding_connect_with_device` accepts the application’s `ID3D11Device` and retains it until close. Passing null, or using `dsh_frame_forwarding_connect`, creates a default device. Every connect function takes the channel's TX credential. `dsh_frame_forwarding_connect_with_options` additionally bounds connection/handshake time, including a wait while a previous producer drains, and accepts a cancellation callback on the connecting thread; a busy channel fails with text starting `channel-busy`. Applications choose their own GPU; DSH selects the transport. Serialize the adopted device’s immediate context with SDK writes. macOS requires a null device.

`dsh_frame_forwarding_trim` returns every idle surface to the receiver's shared byte budget: available surfaces, the queued latest frame, granted allocations not yet created and pending requests; acquired and submitted surfaces stay. Call it when the view stops displaying frames, for example after applying an invisible viewport, and the next acquisition requests allocations again. On Windows it flushes the immediate context of the producer's D3D11 device, because D3D11 destroys released textures only at the next flush; call it on the thread that uses that context. The Office engine trims after acknowledging an invisible viewport.

Acquisition initially returns null while the receiver grants allocation credit. Poll and retry when the owning application is ready; do not spin. Allocation requests enter a shared FIFO budget queue. Grants cover idle pool allocations as well as displayed frames. A null acquisition otherwise indicates exhausted credits; terminal allocation errors are reported by polling with `kind = -1` and explanatory text. Stop processing on a negative poll result and preserve its diagnostic before closing. A consumer must bound its overall operation lifetime and disconnect on timeout.

Textures use top-left BGRA8 premultiplied pixels in sRGB. Windows surfaces have a keyed mutex using key 0. Acquisition grants a lease without locking: SDK CPU uploads own the write lock; external GPU writers own it themselves through `dsh_frame_forwarding_surface_keyed_mutex` or their import API. Writers release key 0 after queueing commands and release imported objects/views before submit or discard. CPU uploads copy the input before returning and do not wait for GPU completion; `dsh_frame_forwarding_write_bgra_with_timeout` bounds mutex acquisition. `AcquireSync` can block the CPU. macOS writers must complete GPU work before submit or discard. Reusing a surface requires both a new acquisition and the write lock on Windows. If GPU access release fails, close the connection without reusing the surface.

Frame IDs must be integers from 1 through 9007199254740991 and unique among outstanding submissions. `dsh_frame_forwarding_submit` returns 1 when submitted and 0 on failure. A failed submission leaves a valid acquisition with the caller for retry or discard under the same GPU completion requirements.

Continuous streams submit with `dsh_frame_forwarding_submit_latest`, which never waits for receiver credit. With `N` the receiver's frame limit, a frame is sent at once while fewer than `max(1, N - 1)` submissions await release; otherwise it becomes the client's single queued frame, and the older queued frame returns to the pool unsent. When polling observes a release, the SDK sends the queued frame, so the receiver gets the newest complete frame without another render or external input. Acquisition reuses the queued surface when no other surface of that size is free, so with `N` of at least 2 an allocated stream always has a target and its application state can advance at its own cadence. Memory stays within the `N` allocations. `dsh_frame_forwarding_submit_latest` marks its frames replaceable, so a relay receiver presents the newest staged stream frame. Request/reply frames keep `dsh_frame_forwarding_submit`, which never drops a frame. Node producers call `submitLatest(frameId, metadata)`.

Windows Vulkan and D3D12 consumers borrow the NT handle through `dsh_frame_forwarding_surface_shared_handle` while the surface is acquired. They must use the SDK's GPU adapter and enable keyed-mutex synchronization in their import API, following the ownership rules above. The SDK owns the handle; callers must not close it. The function returns null on macOS. Receiver copies acquire the source mutex with a bounded timeout when the actual texture descriptor declares one; legacy textures retain the completed-write requirement.

Application JSON, frame correlation, input semantics, viewport generations and input acknowledgements are defined by the consuming application protocol. Control messages are limited to 16383 UTF-8 bytes. The SDK does not expose arbitrary process launching or native handles to webpages. The SDK has no LibreOffice runtime dependency; applications may install Kit with `--omit=optional` when only native rendering is needed.

## Build and validation

Run `node scripts/build.mjs` on the target platform with complete matching Node headers available. The SDK version comes from the public Kit package metadata. Set `DSH_NODE_INCLUDE` explicitly when necessary; Windows additionally requires a developer toolchain environment and `DSH_NODE_LIB`. Builds produce precompiled Node-API and static SDK artifacts with SHA-256 receipts. Installation never invokes a compiler. Public Kit packing requires all four supported targets from one source commit. Partial payloads cannot be packed. The verifier checks addon and static-library architectures, artifact hashes, source hashes, versions, protocol and the `transferable-tx` and `producer-local-handles` capabilities before signing. Desktop runtime packaging retains only the selected target’s frame-forwarding prebuilds, along with the package license.

Run `pnpm test` in this directory after building. `DSH_FRAME_FORWARDING_PACKAGE_ROOT` selects an installed SDK payload for transport and lifecycle tests; diagnostics may be retained outside the package with `DSH_FRAME_FORWARDING_DIAGNOSTICS`. Fixture setup gives each complete compile/link group 120 seconds within a 180-second setup hook; protocol and runner deadlines are separate. Compiler receipts preserve the resolved executable, arguments, working directory, elapsed time, direct-child outcome and stdout/stderr. Compiler descendant exit is not observed. Parent fixtures prepare GPU inspectors and pass their paths only to owned runners, retaining the temporary files until those runners exit. The native CI lane runs C transport and Node producer integration tests serially before packing, including asynchronous shutdown and Worker termination. Performance and Electron shared-texture import require separate actual GPU validation; a successful native transport test alone does not establish those results.

## Browser and Electron presentation

`@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit/frame-forwarding/browser` exports `FrameForwardingFrameDisplay`, `createFrameForwardingFramePainter`, and their types. Importing this entry does not load Electron, Office or native addons and allocates no graphics resources. The generic view identifier preserves application-specific string types. Applications own view creation, authorization, producer control and input arbitration.

`FrameForwardingFrameDisplay.present()` takes ownership of a frame lease and releases it after painting or rejection. Hidden documents wait for visibility; a generation change or disposal cancels the wait. The owner separately updates producer visibility. Dispose the display before removing its canvas.

`@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit/frame-forwarding/electron` exports `detectFrameForwardingAdapter` and `sendFrameForwardingFrame` for Electron Main. Adapter detection waits for complete Chromium GPU information and observes its exported Direct3D11 texture within one supplied deadline. Unsupported backends or software compositing return `null` without creating an offscreen window. Cancellation also covers GPU initialization and window construction. After the application validates the recipient and frame metadata, `sendFrameForwardingFrame` owns the delivery credit through submission failure or Electron's final GPU-reference release. Its completion does not imply GPU release. The required failure callback synchronously stops producer I/O before Main releases its import or returns the delivery credit; the submission promise then rejects.

`@deepseek-ai/libreoffice-kit/frame-forwarding/electron/preload` exports `createFrameForwardingTextureReceiver` for a sandboxed preload. Bundle this entry with Electron external, and install its single document-wide receiver before starting production. Register at most one listener per view. Unsubscribe and revocation stop future deliveries; consumers retain delivered leases until explicit release. Missing consumers, frame extraction failures and throwing listeners release the imported texture. IPC authorization and application lifecycle remain with the caller.

## Distribution

The public Kit package exports the Node SDK, SDK metadata, verifier, browser and Electron entries independently. Resolve the SDK JSON file and read its `header`, `sources`, and `staticLibraries[target]` paths relative to that directory. Normal installation and runtime use the bundled addon without compiling or downloading native binaries.

The browser painters/display, Electron adapter probe and generic texture ownership tests originate from DeepSeek Harness commit `21261bee8b9a820c62c9e42cade3ff644b747a29`, under `packages/client/frame-forwarding` and `apps/desktop`. Their unit tests are maintained with these implementations; DSH retains application integration tests.

The MIT SDK originated in DeepSeek Harness commit `4438b67c13d529c9882d89893ed5cd610ace11cc`. Its WebGPU adapter retains the Office fixes from LibreOffice Kit commit `2ae2de8c7e88df00e74ee538ebd5662f47c7a1df`. The Node binding and standalone C SDK share the source tree used by the Kit engine build. Protocol version 1 is unchanged; the `capabilities` field of `sdk.json`, `receipt.json` and each prebuild manifest records `transferable-tx` and `producer-local-handles`, which distinguish current builds from earlier protocol 1 builds.
